list.listitem: Peritonsillar abscess is a suppurative complication of acute tonsillitis usually seen in children through young adults. Typical presentation consists of severe throat pain, trismus, and tender submandibular lymphadenopathy. C
Diagnosis is by the history and physical (sometimes aided by ultrasound or contrasted CT). C
Outpatient needle aspiration and incision and drainage are equally effective initial management options. A
Abscess gram stain, culture and sensitivity guide antibiotic treatment. C
Tonsillectomy is often recommended for recurrent peritonsillar abscess. B

background.definition: Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) is a suppurative collection in the peritonsillar space between the capsule of the palatine tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx.

list.listitem: 0.3 new cases per 1000 persons/year.
PTA complicates less than 1% of acute pharyngitis episodes.
No gender difference.
Accounts for 30% of soft tissue abscesses in the head and neck.
Can occur in all age groups, most commonly in 20- to 40-year-olds.
Estimated to result in at least $150 million in health care expenditure annually.
Suppurative complication of acute pharyngotonsillitis.
Though PTA is usually polymicrobial, organism most often implicated is group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS).
Although antibiotic usage has declined in the United Kingdom, this has not led to an increase in hospitalizations for peritonsillar abscess.
There is a statistical association between smoking and peritonsillar abscess.
Definitive pathogenesis still unclear.

Thought to be a complication of unresolved acute pharyngotonsillitis and is the endpoint on a continuum of infectious processes beginning with tonsillitis, progressing to cellulitis, and eventually abscess formation.
Some evidence supports mechanism involving abscess formation in Weber's salivary glands in the supratonsillar fossa.
Most commonly the result of polymicrobial infection often involving GABHS.
Other common aerobic organisms associated with abscess formation include Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria species.
Common anaerobes include Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, and Prevotella.
There are no reliable clinical predictors for which patients will develop a complication of pharyngitis.
Diagnosis is usually made by the history and physical examination. C
CT scan of neck with contrast and/or intraoral ultrasound may aid diagnosis. C
Successful aspiration or drainage with subsequent aspirate analysis definitively proves presence of abscess. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Longer prodromal phase, heterophile screen positive
Imaging studies may be needed to differentiate

list.listitem: Common symptoms include sore throat, fatigue/malaise, dysphagia, odynophagia, fever, headache, halitosis, otalgia, drooling, trismus, muffled, or "hot potato" voice.

Typical findings on examination include tender cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, swelling of the anterior pillar and medialization of the affected tonsil, and deviation of the uvula to the contralateral side.
Limited objective data have been published regarding the history and physical examination. One small study of 14 patients found that the clinical impression was 78% sensitive and 50% specific.
Telemedicine diagnosis is viable in peritonsillar abscess.
Imaging is not needed unless diagnosis is uncertain.

Intraoral ultrasound showing hypoechoic cavity with a well-defined circumference is moderately accurate (LR+ 3, LR− 0.13). It is better at ruling out PTA when negative than ruling it in when positive.
Ultrasound, especially intraoral, is accurate and can help rule in (LR+ 3.6) or rule out (LR- 0.1) the diagnosis. POCUS was similar in accuracy to radiologist performed ultrasound.
CT with contrast is another option to confirm the diagnosis if uncertain.
Diagnosis is based on history and physical examination.
Imaging with intraoral ultrasound or CT with contrast is recommended only if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Aspirate culture and analysis should guide antibiotic choice.
Needle aspiration followed by appropriate antibiotic coverage is as effective as and less invasive than incision and drainage. B
Antibiotic coverage should be initiated with consideration for typical causative organisms and further guided by abscess Gram stain and culture. C
Steroids may shorten time to resolution of several symptoms without increasing complications. B
Appropriate selection of antibiotic therapy should be guided by abscess Gram, stain, culture, and sensitivity.
One small study found that IM clindamycin was equivalent to IV ampicillin/sulbactam.
One small RCT found improved outcomes with corticosteroids.
A systematic review of 3 RCTs concluded that adding metronidzaole to penicillin does not provide additional benefit.
Needle aspiration and incision and drainage are options for treatment of a first episode.
Tonsillectomy with open abscess drainage ("quinsy tonsillectomy") or I&D followed several weeks later by tonsillectomy ("interval tonsillectomy") are options for patients with recurrent PTA.
A systematic review of 18 studies found a pooled prevalence of post quinsy tonsillectomy bleeding of 6.6%, with a return to the operating theater rate of only 2.4%.
Three good quality RCTs with a total of 162 compared needle aspiration with I&D and found no difference in outcomes.

Two high-quality RCTs with a total of 104 patients compared quinsy tonsillectomy with interval tonsillectomy and found no difference in clinical outcomes but a longer hospital stay for interval tonsillectomy (resulting from rehospitalization at a later date for the subsequent tonsillectomy).
Consider hospitalization or consultation with otolaryngologist if there is potential for airway obstruction.
Other complications include abscess rupture, local extension of abscess to involve the parapharyngeal space, bacteremia, and other associated poststreptococcal complications.
Complications described after treatment for peritonsillar abscess include descending mediastinitis, para and retropharyngeal abscess, and necrotizing fascitiitis.
Recurrence rate following a single episode of peritonsillar abscess is 15% to 20%. B
